strengths: LPAM addresses a practical stitching problem: seam selection alone cannot repair local geometric misalignment. Its modular design offers a useful way to improve existing pipelines without retraining.

Tables 1–2 report consistent improvements across 79 image pairs, four seam-cutting methods, and five alignment methods, including UDIS++. For example, adding LPAM to the REW-based baseline increases SEAGULL SSIM from 0.638 to 0.697.

The visual examples demonstrate useful repairs to structural discontinuities. The sigmoid and patch-size ablations provide supporting evidence, and the discussion candidly identifies failures involving small patches.
The pipeline is understandable from Figure 2 and Algorithm 1. Established components and public datasets are cited, key parameters and hardware are reported, and a code repository is linked.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation does not adequately establish overall mosaic quality. All four metrics measure agreement around the selected seam, overlooking distortions and discontinuities elsewhere. Table 3 exposes this limitation: removing the sigmoid improves RMSE, SSIM, and ZNCC on every dataset despite introducing boundary artifacts in Figure 3. The qualitative evidence is useful, but systematic boundary-quality or perceptual evaluation and per-image degradation rates are needed to substantiate the broader quality and robustness claims.

The scientific advance over existing seam-guided alignment is insufficiently established. The method combines established SSIM, Otsu thresholding, SIFT flow, and graph-cut components. Its practical integration has merit, but the claimed new paradigm needs clearer differentiation from SEAGULL [22] and dense-matching-based seam estimation [35]. Comparisons with seam-guided alternatives are largely qualitative, and there is no controlled comparison against dense-flow refinement over an entire seam band to isolate the benefit of selective patch repair.

The seam-acceptance rule in Section 3.2 can skip severely misaligned inputs. If every seam pixel has Q = 0.8, corresponding to SSIM = 0.2, then max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q), and the seam is accepted without refinement. Thus the criterion detects relative outliers rather than absolute alignment quality. This directly limits the claimed independence from initial alignment, especially when errors extend along much of the seam.

The smoothness claim exceeds what the construction guarantees. The x-dependent sigmoid in Eqs. (4–5) does not enforce displacement compatibility on every boundary segment where a warped target patch meets the unmodified target image. Fixing graph-cut boundary labels ensures label consistency, not geometric continuity. Figure 6 acknowledges a resulting failure, but its prevalence and the method's applicability to other seam geometries are not established.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence remain incomplete in the supplied manuscript. Patch padding, overlapping-patch handling, SIFT-flow settings, image resolutions, and acquisition/release details for the new dataset are insufficiently specified. Table 4 reports LPAM time separately and excludes initial alignment; the roughly 7–10 seconds of added CPU processing do not establish an efficiency advantage over broader refinement or seam-guided alternatives.
